input:
A level loop holds the level in a process vessel at the value set for it, and this tutorial explains the loop through its parts in turn: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback. The outcome is a loop that acts against every departure of the level from its set point, .

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and transmits the measurement to the controller as a signal that follows the level. The sensor reads the contents of the vessel only and takes no action on the process, and the accuracy of the loop rests on the accuracy of that reading.

The controller compares the measured level with the set point and calculates a correction from the difference between them, the error. A level above the set point and a level below it produce corrections in opposite senses, and the size of the correction follows the size of the error. The controller moves nothing in the process; its output is an instruction to the part that does.

The final element is the part that acts on the process. In this loop it is a control valve on the inlet line to the vessel, and the correction from the controller sets the opening of the valve, and with the opening the flow into the vessel.

The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise of level above the set point moves the valve towards closed and reduces the inflow, so the action of the loop opposes the change that produced it; a fall of level opens the valve, raises the inflow, and again acts in opposition. A loop arranged with the opposite sign would drive the level away from the set point instead of returning it. Controller settings are outside the structure set out here.
